# Introduction to the Business Problem

We have been using the Credit data in class. For this lab, treat the 400
rows as credit-card accounts on QNB (Qatar National Bank) cards. The
outcome is `Balance`: the average amount on the card, in dollars. Mean
Balance on this file is about $520. Ninety accounts sit at zero.

QNB has already issued the cards. For each account we observe income,
credit limit, credit rating, number of cards, age, years of education,
whether the person owns a home, is married, is a student, and region
(East, South, or West). That is many predictors, so there are many
possible least-squares models. If we put every predictor into one fit,
or we keep adding predictors because the training fit looks better, we
can overfit these 400 accounts. A closer fit here does not mean the
model will predict well for a new customer.

The question for the hour is the one from class: how can we select a
good predictive model for Balance among many, and how can we avoid
overfitting?

We will search with three methods from class: best subset, forward
stepwise, and backward stepwise. That gives the best model of each size.
Then we will pick a size in the two ways we discussed.

- Cp, AIC, BIC, and adjusted $R^2$ adjust the training error. We will
  compute those on all 400 accounts and label that fact.
- Cross-validation scores accounts we did not use to pick the
  predictors. We will do that only on the 280 training accounts.

Do not pick predictors from the $p$-values of the model that uses every
predictor. We will see why that fails when two predictors move together.

Open the case PDF before you run code and keep the codebook in view.
Income is in thousands of dollars. Balance, Limit are in dollars. Rating
is in points. `Student`, `Own`, and `Married` are Yes/No. `Region` is
East, South, or West.

**Think 1.** Why can a model that fits these 400 accounts very well still
be a poor model for the next QNB customer?

**Think 2.** Ninety accounts have Balance exactly zero, and the mean is
about $520. What should you keep in mind when you read a least-squares
slope on this file?

```{.r .cell-code}
# leaps: regsubsets() for best subset, forward, and backward search.
# ggplot2 / patchwork / scales: figures that we can read in the room.
# Why? Base par(mfrow) stacks plots. patchwork keeps the comparison
# aligned and labeled, which is the point of the criteria panel later.
if (!requireNamespace("leaps", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("leaps")
}
if (!requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("ggplot2")
}
if (!requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("patchwork")
}
if (!requireNamespace("scales", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("scales")
}

library(leaps)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(scales)

options(scipen = 999)

# Dollar-scale RMSE. Why? Balance is in dollars. A unitless MSE is
# harder to hold next to the $520 mean.
rmse <- function(y, yhat) {
  sqrt(mean((y - yhat)^2))
}

# Names of the predictors in a regsubsets() model of a given size.
# Why? We will compare teams often. One helper keeps the output short.
selected_at <- function(object, size) {
  setdiff(names(coef(object, id = size)), "(Intercept)")
}
```
:::

# Best Subset Selection

Best subset, for each size $k$, finds the $k$ predictors that minimize
training RSS. It is a search over teams, not a search over $p$-values.

As we add predictors the fit can follow the 280 more closely (lower
bias) and also follow noise (higher variance). The outmat is the team
sheet. An asterisk means that predictor is in the best model of that
size.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# nvmax = 11 because Region has three levels (two dummies) and the
# three Yes/No variables each contribute one dummy. That is 11
# predictors after dummy coding, not 10 raw names.
# Why? If nvmax is too small, we never see the kitchen-sink team and
# the criteria plots get cut off.
best_train <- regsubsets(Balance ~ ., data = train, nvmax = 11)
best_train_sum <- summary(best_train)
best_train_sum$outmat
```

```{.r .cell-code}
# Optional picture of the same outmat. Dark tiles are selected.
# Why? A table is precise. A tile plot makes the Limit / Rating swap
# and the late arrival of Education visible from across the room.
om <- best_train_sum$outmat
best_tiles <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(om)), function(i) {
    data.frame(
      size = i,
      predictor = colnames(om),
      selected = om[i, ] == "*",
      row.names = NULL
    )
  })
)
best_tiles$predictor <- factor(best_tiles$predictor, levels = colnames(om))

ggplot(best_tiles, aes(x = size, y = predictor, fill = selected)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#156082", "FALSE" = "#e8eef2"),
                    labels = c("TRUE" = "In the team", "FALSE" = "Out")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:11) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of predictors",
    y = NULL,
    fill = NULL,
    title = "Best subset on the 280 training accounts",
    subtitle = "Each row is a predictor (after dummy coding). Dark = selected at that size."
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
```

# Forward Stepwise Selection

Forward stepwise starts at the intercept and adds one predictor at a
time. Once a predictor is in, it stays. The search is nested by
construction.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fwd_train_sum <- summary(fwd_train)
fwd_train_sum$outmat
```

# Backward Stepwise Selection

Backward stepwise starts from the model that uses every predictor and
drops the one whose removal hurts training RSS the least. The path is
nested in the other direction.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bwd_train <- regsubsets(Balance ~ ., data = train, nvmax = 11, method = "backward")
bwd_train_sum <- summary(bwd_train)
```

# Training Error by Model Size

Training RMSE is the in-sample fit of the best model of each size on
the 280. It should fall as we add predictors. That is why it cannot
choose a size.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mm_train <- model.matrix(Balance ~ ., data = train)
train_rmse <- sapply(1:11, function(i) {
  cf <- coef(best_train, id = i)
  pred <- as.numeric(mm_train[, names(cf), drop = FALSE] %*% cf)
  rmse(train$Balance, pred)
})

train_err <- data.frame(size = 1:11, rmse = train_rmse)
train_err
```

# Model Comparison (Cp, AIC, BIC, Adjusted R²)

These are the criteria from class that adjust training error. We compute
them on **all 400 accounts** and we label that. They are not an estimate
of error on new customers. They are a ranking of sizes on the file we
already have.

leaps reports Cp, BIC, and adjusted $R^2$. AIC we get by refitting the
best model of each size with `lm()`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Why? The outline for the hour is: criteria on all 400, labeled;
# cross-validation on the 280. Mixing those two without a label is
# how people later claim an "honest" number that used every account.
best_all <- regsubsets(Balance ~ ., data = credit, nvmax = 11)
best_all_sum <- summary(best_all)

aic_vals <- numeric(11)
mm_all <- model.matrix(Balance ~ ., data = credit)
for (i in 1:11) {
  cf <- coef(best_all, id = i)
  vars <- setdiff(names(cf), "(Intercept)")
  dat_i <- data.frame(
    Balance = credit$Balance,
    mm_all[, vars, drop = FALSE],
    check.names = FALSE
  )
  aic_vals[i] <- AIC(lm(Balance ~ ., data = dat_i))
}

crit <- data.frame(
  size = 1:11,
  Cp = as.numeric(best_all_sum$cp),
  AIC = aic_vals,
  BIC = as.numeric(best_all_sum$bic),
  adjR2 = as.numeric(best_all_sum$adjr2)
)
```

```{.r .cell-code}
# Why not select by p-values?
# 1. A p-value in a joint model asks a conditional question: does this
#    predictor help given the others already in the equation? That is
#    not a search over models.
# 2. When two predictors move together, the same slope can look
#    decisive alone and look like noise once its twin is in the room.
# 3. A small p-value can sit next to almost no gain in fit. Look at
#    R^2 and RSE for Rating alone versus Limit + Rating.
#
# Interpret: Alone, Limit and Rating each look like the model. Together,
# one slope keeps a small p-value and the other does not. The RSE of
# the two-predictor fit is not an improvement on Rating alone.
#
# Question: If you had only starred coefficients from the kitchen-sink
# model, would you have kept both Limit and Rating? Why is that a
# bad selection rule on this file?
#
# Discuss: Someone says "Rating is significant, Limit is not, so drop
# Limit." What did they condition on? What would they have said if
# they had run the two simple models first?
#
# Business implication: Do not let a software star decide a credit
# model when the two strongest scores are nearly the same number
# twice. Selection is a comparison of models, not a row of p-values.
```

# Choosing Among Models with Cross-Validation

The criteria above used all 400 accounts. Cross-validation on the 280
is the second way from class: score accounts that were not used to pick
the team of a given size.

`regsubsets()` has no `predict()` method, so we add one. The helper
rebuilds the model matrix, lines up the coefficients, and multiplies.
We then run best subset **inside each training fold**. That is the
step people skip, and it is the step that keeps selection from leaking
across the fold.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Why? Without this helper we would have to rebuild the matrix math
# in every fold. The function is the same idea as predict(lm()):
# new accounts in, fitted Balance out, for a chosen size.
predict.regsubsets <- function(object, newdata, id, ...) {
  form <- as.formula(object$call[[2]])
  mat <- model.matrix(form, newdata)
  coefi <- coef(object, id = id)
  xvars <- names(coefi)
  mat[, xvars] %*% coefi
}
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 10-fold CV over size, on the 280 only.
# Why a new set.seed(46704)? The fold assignment is random. Fixing it
# means the room is looking at the same picture. It is not a claim
# that this fold cut is magic.
k <- 10
set.seed(46704)
folds <- sample(rep(1:k, length = nrow(train)))
cv_mse <- matrix(NA, k, 11, dimnames = list(NULL, paste(1:11)))

for (j in 1:k) {
  # Selection happens on 9 folds only.
  fold_fit <- regsubsets(
    Balance ~ .,
    data = train[folds != j, ],
    nvmax = 11
  )
  for (i in 1:11) {
    pred <- predict(fold_fit, train[folds == j, ], id = i)
    y_fold <- train$Balance[folds == j]
    cv_mse[j, i] <- mean((y_fold - pred)^2)
  }
}

# Average MSE across folds, then take the square root so the axis is
# in dollars. Why? That matches how we have been reading training RMSE.
cv_rmse <- sqrt(colMeans(cv_mse))
cv_rmse
```

# Choosing a Model

We need one model we are willing to take off the 280 accounts. BIC on
the 400 preferred a small model. CV on the 280 is already flat in that
neighborhood. We take the size-4 best-subset team and fit it with
`lm()` on the training accounts.

The 120 held-out accounts stay closed. We are not reporting a test
RMSE in this notebook.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Size 4 on the 280: Income, Limit, Cards, Student.
# Why this size? It is BIC's pick on the 400, and it sits in the
# flat CV region on the 280. Size 6 can win a CV minimum by a
# fraction of a dollar. That is not a strong argument for the
# extra predictors on a $520 outcome.
chosen <- lm(Balance ~ Income + Limit + Cards + Student, data = train)
summary(chosen)
```
